chunks: SI/PI simulation experience. The question: Do you have any SI/PI simulation experience?
The interviewer is not asking for a tool list.
They want to know what you actually simulated, what the result told you, and whether you understand that a simulation is only as good as its models.
Signal integrity (SI) simulation checks that signals arrive clean. Power integrity (PI) simulation checks that the supply stays steady ("What SI/PI are and why they matter").
Be honest about how much hands-on work you have done.
A good answer reads like a very short lab report.
It names the question, the tool, one number that surprised you, the design change that followed, and one thing you would not trust yet.
A small honest experiment, checked against a hand calculation, beats naming five tools you never used.
The professional workflow. A good answer touches several of these boxes, even if your own experience covers only the first two or three.
Model: the simplified stand-in a simulator uses for a real part or wire. What it leaves out is where simulations mislead.
Hand check: a quick pencil calculation that you compare with the simulator's answer to catch mistakes.
Pre-layout / post-layout: simulating before the board is drawn to pick a design, versus after, to verify the real routing.
Correlation: comparing the simulation with a measurement on real hardware to see whether the model can be trusted.
A skeleton to fill in with your own story:. "In [project or course] I wanted to understand [problem, such as ringing on a fast output] .
I modeled it in [tool] with [what you modeled] and compared it with a hand calculation, which predicted [number] . The simulation gave [number] .
That led me to [change you made] . What I would not trust is [model limit] , so on a real board I would [check or correlate against measurement] ."
That is the whole idea: question, result, decision, limits.
"[Honest version of your experience.]
For example, I simulated a driver, 50 ohm transmission line and capacitive load in LTspice and checked it against the bounce diagram: with a 20 ohm source into an open line the load overshoots to 4.
7 volts from a 3. 3 volts step and rings, and adding a 30 ohm series resistor matches the source to the line and removes it.
I know the limits: ideal models, no package parasitics.
In a real design I'd use IBIS or S-parameter models, extract the layout, simulate pre- and post-layout and correlate against a TDR or eye measurement."
